title: To the tune of a king's ballad
hookLine: the heading says it's sung to the tune of a folk ballad about a king, and ragis sing it with chhants between

lines: A HYMN ON A BORROWED TUNE.
EVERYONE ALREADY KNOWS HOW IT GOES.
THE HEADING ABOVE ASA DI VAR.
cards: Plenty of hymns borrowed their tunes from somewhere else: a melody from a tavern, a folk song everybody's grandmother knew, a march from a parade ground.
Give it new words, and suddenly a whole room can sing along, because they already know how it goes. The trick is old, and it's everywhere.
Above the first line of Asa di Var in the Guru Granth Sahib, there's a heading that's easy to skip right past. It names the old tune to use.

teach.b: The heading says, in paraphrase: Asa, the first Guru. A var, with saloks, and saloks also written by the first Guru, to be sung to the tune of Tunda Asraj.
Dhunee is the word for tune. Tunda Asraj was the subject of a folk ballad people in Punjab knew: Asraj, a king, often described as tunda, maimed or one-handed.

The story is told in more than one version, usually about a prince who's wronged and wounded but rises to rule. The Guru Granth Sahib doesn't retell it. It just names the tune and expects the singer to know how it goes.
That's the striking thing. The heading doesn't point to a sacred melody only the trained could sing.
It points to a folk tune ordinary people already carried in their heads, and the var gives it new words: words about God as the true King, and about the inner battle.
Some other vars in the Guru Granth Sahib carry similar headings, naming the folk tunes they were meant to follow. Then there's how it's sung today.
Ragis usually pair Asa di Var with the chhants of Guru Ram Das, the fourth Guru, also in raag Asa.
A chhant is sung, then a pauri with its saloks, then the next chhant, so the fourth Guru's verses and the first Guru's ballad take turns.
Three Gurus' voices, braided together, at dawn.

how: The heading of Asa di Var names the folk tune of Tunda Asraj, and ragis sing it each morning interwoven with the chhants of Guru Ram Das.

o: a tune, the melody a hymn is sung to
the echo of a gong in a temple
a drumbeat that keeps soldiers marching

games.q: to the tune of a king's ballad — tap the pairs.
p: the king in the folk ballad
Guru Ram Das's verses, sung between

s: Asa di Var's heading names a folk tune to sing it to
the tune of Tunda Asraj, a ballad people already knew.
the Guru Granth Sahib retells the story of Asraj in full
it only names the tune; the story is told in more than one version outside it.
Asa di Var is usually sung alone, with nothing in between
ragis weave in Guru Ram Das's chhants between the pauris.

games.q: you want a whole village to sing a new song about God. what does the heading of Asa di Var suggest?
o: invent a melody only experts can sing.
use a folk tune everyone already knows.
don't use any tune at all.
games.why: the heading names the tune of Tunda Asraj, a folk ballad people carried in their heads, and gives it new words.

practice: Hum a melody you've known for years, a lullaby, a song from childhood, something your family sang in the car, softly and slowly, noticing how the next note arrives before you think.
Then let the humming fade and sit with the quiet it leaves; if you pray, let Waheguru ride on the tune as you hum.

wordCard.voice: Dhunee, tune or melody: Asa di Var's heading names the dhunee of Tunda Asraj, an old melody, given new words about God.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: dhunee, tune or melody; the heading names the dhunee of Tunda Asraj.

carryVoice: Your line: old tunes, new words. A folk song everyone knew, carrying new words about God. That's day five hundred thirty-seven.
